**Coordinator (Claude) — decision after round 1**

**Where things stand after round 1:** Codex and Claude independently arrived at essentially the same MoSCoW shape, which is a good sign this cut is right rather than just persuasive. Both treat the entire MVP slice locked in `next_steps_small` as the must-have core — auth persistence, zero-dead-end pod join/create, no-PII request posting, real APNs delivery, server-side CAS accept-race with the explicit "already covered by [name]" loser, release/reopen, the new `withdrawn` state, still-open aging, and the completion receipt — and both keep the same won't-build list (chat/DM, location/GPS, payments, recurring/scheduled requests, history feed, admin console beyond code-rotate, moderation, child PII, background-check-style badges). Both also agree the acceptance bar is the two-device demo, not an isolated checklist.

Two things Claude raised this round that Codex hasn't reacted to yet, so they're not locked:

1. **Internal tiering of the must-have list.** Claude wants it written down explicitly that if build time gets tight, the "tier one" items (auth, pod join/create with both empty states, no-PII post, real APNs delivery, and the accept-race CAS resolution) are the ones that absolutely cannot be rushed, while "tier two" musts (release/reopen, withdraw, still-open aging, completion/receipt) are still required but can absorb rough edges before tier one ever does. This doesn't change what's must-have, just the order sacrifices would come in — but it needs Codex's sign-off since it's a build-priority claim, not just a feature list.
2. **Subscription/paywall status.** Claude wants it stated plainly that the three subscription unlocks locked back in `per_app_product_brief` (multi-pod, receipt export, critical-alert bypass) are should/could-at-best for this build — data model can leave room for an entitlement flag, but no StoreKit integration, no paywall screen, nothing gated is in scope for what actually gets built and graded. Codex's list simply didn't mention subscription features at all, so this isn't a disagreement so much as an unaddressed gap that needs to be closed explicitly so nobody burns build time on in-app-purchase plumbing.

Both participants also agree acceptance criteria need to be literal and testable (e.g., "kill network mid-accept-tap, confirm no false-confirmed state on reconnect" rather than "handle errors gracefully"), and that the fleet's recorded failure patterns (blank placeholder screens, hardcoded color/font literals instead of the theme file) need to be explicitly guarded against here given this app's four-state and dark-mode requirements.

CONSENSUS: NO

Next round: Codex should confirm or push back on the must-have tiering (tier one vs tier two) and explicitly confirm the subscription/paywall downgrade to should/could-with-no-implementation for this build.

**Codex (Design Lead · Skeptic) — Round 2**

I agree with your build-priority point, Claude, but I want the trade-off explicit: if time gets tight, we can lower finish quality on non-demo flows, not drop correctness. In this phase the literal two-device race demo is the spine, so Tier-1 for that is: sign-in with forced session persistence, zero-dead-end pod onboarding (create or join), post of a same-day request with no child PII, honest await-ack behavior on post, real APNs deep-linked delivery to a second device, and CAS-race arbitration that yields one confirmed + one explicit already-covered transition from server truth. If those are not rock-solid, everything else is moot.

Tier-2 musts absolutely stay in the build contract, not off the table, but they can be intentionally shipped at a minimum-viable fidelity when we’re timing out: release/reopen with re-notify, requester-only withdrawn terminal state, still-open elapsed-time re-broadcast behavior, and receipt/audit generation. The biggest risk if we misclassify these is we accidentally teach users the wrong mental model later, so I want explicit language: “degraded visual polish first, not degraded state semantics.”

On the subscription note, I’m confirming your interpretation, and I’m making it stricter: for v1 build, those three unlocks (multi-pod, exportable/signed history, critical-alert bypass) are out of implementation scope entirely. No StoreKit wiring, no paywall, no entitlement-gated core behavior. We can keep entitlement fields in the schema only if they are inert and clearly unused. If someone tries to frame this as a must feature, that breaks our trust loop because it delays the only thing that proves backend load-bearing behavior: the two-device real-time flow.

One additional correction to avoid later scope bleed: we should treat “all must-have features are testable and required” as unchanged by tiering. Tiering is execution order only, not optionality. If time runs out before completion, we do not ship incomplete state-machine paths that can create false certainty; we ship rougher UX copy or transitions for release/withdraw/still-open, but the state transitions and server invariants remain real.

**Claude (QA & Risk · Pragmatist) — Round 2**

Codex, your requirements contract is genuinely stronger than what I sketched — REQ-01 through REQ-18 map cleanly onto every locked decision, and I don't see anything in your must/should/could split that contradicts mine. But I want to push on three specific things rather than just say "agreed" and move on, because agreeing too fast is how a phase like this ships something with a soft spot nobody named.

First, you filed "theme token system in one Theme.swift file and guaranteed dark-mode semantic rendering for all core screens" under should (S06 in your list). I think that's wrong, and not as a matter of taste — look at the fleet anti-pattern history sitting right in front of us: two named design_lint incidents, one citing a raw_font_size hardcoded literal, one citing an inline_color hardcoded literal in a Theme.swift file that apparently existed but wasn't actually used consistently. That's not a hypothetical risk, that's this exact team having shipped this exact mistake before. The global app-build rules also state it flatly: implement the design spec's tokens as one theme file and reference it everywhere, never scatter literals through views, and every app must fully support dark mode with semantic color roles verified in both appearances. That's not "important but not required to prove core reliability," that's a hard global rule with a documented failure history. I'd move it to must, and I'd word it precisely enough that it's actually checkable: no font size, spacing value, or color literal outside Theme.swift, and every core screen screenshot-verified in both light and dark. The coordinator's draft requirements-json already has this as R-035 marked core:true, which I think is the correct call — so if that carries forward, we should also correct your should-list wording to match rather than leave a contradiction between the requirements contract and the feature MoSCoW list sitting in the same phase output.

Second — the tiering point the coordinator flagged as unconfirmed. I want to make the case sharper rather than just repeat it, because I think there's a version of "we're aligned" that's actually hiding a disagreement: your must list treats REQ-06 (withdraw) and REQ-05 (accept race) as equally weighted line items, and technically they should both pass for the app to be "done." But they are not equally dangerous if one slips. If the build runs long and something in the withdraw flow is half-wired — say the re-notify push doesn't fire but the state machine correctly blocks a stale accept — that's a real bug, but the app still doesn't lie to anyone; nobody gets a false "confirmed" or a false "already covered." If something in the accept-race CAS path is half-wired, the entire premise of the app is dead: two phones show two different truths, or worse, both show "confirmed." Those aren't the same category of failure, and I don't think "everything on the must list is must" captures that asymmetry. I'm not proposing to make anything not-must — I'm proposing the phase output say explicitly, in the requirements contract itself, which requirements are demo-fatal (R-009, R-010, R-011, R-017 in the coordinator's numbering — the CAS mechanism, the deterministic winner/loser split, no-optimistic-UI, and honest delivery copy) versus which are must-but-recoverable-if-rough (withdraw, release timing, still-open aging, receipt polish). That way if a build agent has to make a triage call under time pressure at 11pm, the document itself tells them which corner is unacceptable to cut, instead of leaving that judgment call to whoever's tired and behind schedule.

Third, small but I think it matters: your REQ-01 says a seeded pod member must receive the push "immediately" — I'd flag that word specifically because it's exactly the kind of soft language that becomes an argument later about whether something's "close enough." APNs delivery timing is not something the app controls end-to-end; Apple's push infrastructure is best-effort, and we already accepted a version of this uncertainty when we locked the honest "sent to N members" copy instead of a delivery guarantee. I'd rather the acceptance criterion be split into what we actually control (server commits the CAS write and submits the push payload to APNs within some tight bound, say a couple seconds) versus what we're observing but not guaranteeing (actual device receipt, which the two-phone demo will show empirically but which isn't a hard contractual number we can fail a build on if Apple's infrastructure has a slow moment during the demo). Otherwise we've quietly reintroduced an "it must always work perfectly end-to-end including a third party's infrastructure" requirement that nobody can actually promise, which is a bad thing to put in a document we're going to grade adherence against later.

On subscription — glad to see the coordinator's draft requirements-json already reflects the should/could-no-implementation framing as R-038, but I want that said out loud and locked as an actual decision this round, not just something that appeared correctly in a JSON draft because nobody objected. Codex, your list simply didn't mention subscription at all, which I read as tacit agreement rather than disagreement, but tacit isn't the same as locked — I'd like you to say it plainly so it's an actual cross-confirmed decision and not something that just quietly survived because it wasn't contradicted.

**Where things stand after round 2:** Codex came back and locked the two things left hanging from round 1. On tiering, Codex confirmed Claude's split but sharpened it in an important way: Tier-1 (auth persistence, zero-dead-end onboarding, no-PII posting with awaiting-confirmation, real APNs deep-link delivery, and the CAS accept-race resolving to confirmed/already-covered) is the literal spine of the two-phone demo and can't be soft; Tier-2 (release/reopen, withdrawn, still-open aging, completion/receipt) stays fully required in the graded contract, but if time runs out, what gets sacrificed there is visual polish, never state-machine correctness. Codex was explicit that tiering is a scheduling tool, not a way to quietly ship a broken invariant with nicer UI around it — no Tier-2 feature can drop its correct state transitions to save time, only its finish. On subscriptions, Codex went further than a simple confirmation: multi-pod, receipt export, and critical-alert bypass are now explicitly zero build effort for this slice — no StoreKit, no paywall UI, no gated core behavior, entitlement fields in the schema only if they stay inert. Both sides are aligned here.

But Claude's round-2 message raised three fresh points Codex hasn't had a chance to react to, so this isn't fully closed yet:

1. **Theme/dark-mode belongs on must, not should.** Codex's MoSCoW list filed the tokenized theme file and full dark-mode coverage under "should" (S06), but the requirements-json already has it as core:true, and the fleet's own recorded failure history has two dedicated design-lint incidents (hardcoded font size, hardcoded color) that are exactly this mistake. Claude wants Codex's feature list corrected to match the requirements contract rather than leaving a should/must contradiction sitting in the same phase output.
2. **Name the demo-fatal subset explicitly, inside the requirements document itself.** Claude isn't proposing new tiers beyond what Codex already locked — she's asking that the CAS mechanism, the deterministic winner/loser split, the no-optimistic-UI rule, and the honest delivery-count copy be explicitly flagged in-document as "unacceptable to cut" for a build agent making a judgment call late at night, rather than leaving that inference to whoever's tired and behind schedule.
3. **Soften the APNs delivery-timing language.** "Delivers immediately" quietly promises something nobody can guarantee — Apple's push infrastructure is best-effort. Claude wants the requirement split into what the backend actually controls (committing the CAS write and submitting the push payload within a tight, server-owned bound) versus what the two-phone demo observes but isn't graded as a hard contractual number (actual device receipt time).

None of these contradict anything Codex said — they're refinements Codex simply hasn't confirmed yet — so this isn't resolved.

CONSENSUS: NO

Next round: Codex should (1) fix the should/must mismatch on the theme/dark-mode item, (2) confirm explicit demo-fatal tagging of the CAS/no-optimistic/delivery-honesty requirements within the contract, and (3) confirm the reworded APNs timing split (server-controlled commit bound vs. empirically-observed-not-guaranteed device receipt).
